questions.question: Three fair coins are flipped, and f(ω) is the number of heads in outcome ω. Which description of f is most accurate?
options: A variable whose value changes randomly over time
A fixed function from outcomes to numbers. The randomness is in which outcome occurs
An event containing all outcomes with heads
questions.explanation: A random variable is neither random nor a variable. It is a deterministic function S → ℝ, so f(HTH) is always 2.

questions.question: g = 1 if the first coin is heads, and h = 1 if all three coins match. Why are g and h independent?
options: Because they are defined using different coins
Because Pr[g = x and h = y] = Pr[g = x]·Pr[h = y] for every pair of values, e.g. Pr[g=1, h=1] = 1/8 = ½·¼
questions.explanation: Independence of RVs means the product rule holds for all value pairs. Being indicators doesn't guarantee it, and h does depend on coin 1. It just isn't shifted by it.

questions.question: R is the number of heads in 10 independent coins with heads probability p. Which formula gives Pr[R = 3]?
questions.explanation: Each sequence with 3 heads has probability p³(1−p)⁷ by mutual independence, and there are C(10, 3) such sequences. C(10,3)/2¹⁰ is only correct when p = ½.

questions.question: In the candy-box game, why does choosing a random threshold guarantee at least a 55% win rate?
options: With probability at least 1/10 the threshold separates the boxes, giving a sure win. Otherwise you still win half the time
Because the bigger box always has more than 5 candies
Because a random choice wins 55% of the time in any game
questions.explanation: By the law of total probability, Pr[win] ≥ 1·(1/10) + ½·(9/10) = 0.55, whatever counts the boxes contain.
